strengths: Strong motivation and elegant concept: Inspired by cognitive science, the idea of training a robot to grasp complex, unseen objects using only procedurally generated and 3D-printed primitive-based 'Cézanne toys' is highly intuitive, elegant, and well-executed.

Impressive real-world generalizability: The model achieves a 66.67% zero-shot success rate on 64 YCB objects on a real Franka robot and 50.77% on a real H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands, showing excellent sim-to-real and toy-to-real transfer.

Extensive real-world and multi-embodiment evaluation: Testing on both parallel-jaw grippers (Franka Panda) and five-fingered dexterous hands (H1-2 humanoid) demonstrates the robustness and versatility of the proposed method across different action/state spaces.

Thorough and insightful ablation studies: The paper contains exceptional analysis evaluating the impact of the number of unique toys, number of demonstrations, primitive shapes, colors, toy complexity, and model scales, providing valuable scaling insights for robotic learning.

High data and model efficiency: Unlike large-scale vision-language-action (VLA) models, the proposed policy is trained from scratch with very few demonstrations (1500 for Franka, 500 for H1-2) and a small parameter size (86M), yet outperforms much larger models in zero-shot generalization.
weaknesses: Relatively straightforward technical novelty: The primary architectural component, DetPool, is a combination of attention masking using SAM 2 masks and mean pooling. While highly effective, the concept of masking out background attention in Vision Transformers is relatively standard in computer vision.

Robustness to segmentation quality: The method heavily relies on accurate segmentation masks (from SAM 2 / Faster R-CNN). In real-world scenarios with heavy clutter, occlusions, shadows, or reflective objects, segmentation can be noisy. The paper does not thoroughly evaluate the policy's sensitivity to imperfect or noisy masks.

Task scope is limited to basic grasping: The paper focuses purely on the single-stage task of picking and lifting. How this toy-based training approach scales to more complex, multi-stage, or non-prehensile manipulation tasks remains unexplored.

Baseline comparison: On the real Franka robot, the fine-tuned π0-FAST baseline still outperforms LEGO (76.56% vs 66.67%). Although LEGO is much smaller and trained from scratch with significantly less pretraining, it does not achieve the highest absolute success rate among the compared methods.

strengths: Highly intuitive and biologically inspired concept: Training robots to grasp novel complex objects by learning exclusively on randomly composed shape primitives ('Cezanne toys'), which is inspired by how infants learn to manipulate.

Extensive physical robot validation: The method is evaluated on both a parallel-jaw gripper (Franka) and a humanoid with a multi-finger dexterous hand (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire hands) across real-world datasets (YCB and everyday items).

Rigorous scaling and ablation analyses: The paper provides thorough scaling studies on the number of unique toys vs. demonstrations, model sizes, colors, and primitive types, providing valuable insights for future research.

Effective representation learning: The proposed Detection Pooling (DetPool) mechanism utilizes SAM 2 attention masking inside a ViT encoder to obtain clean, object-centric features, which is shown to be crucial for generalization.
weaknesses: Dependency on a robust object detector/segmenter: During real-world testing, DetPool relies on Faster R-CNN and SAM 2 to mask out non-object tokens. Any segmentation or detection failure would directly degrade policy performance. The paper does not thoroughly discuss how sensitive the policy is to noisy masks or detection failures.

Clarification on detector training: In Appendix E, the authors mention training a Faster R-CNN on 200 annotated toy images to obtain bounding boxes. It is unclear if this detector generalizes zero-shot to the YCB evaluation objects or if it had to be trained/fine-tuned on YCB objects as well. If it requires training for new objects, it reduces the 'zero-shot' claim of the policy.

Performance compared to pre-trained VLAs: While the method is much more data-efficient and has a smaller model footprint (86M parameters), the fine-tuned π0-FAST (3B parameters) still outperforms LEGO by ~10% in the real-world Franka experiments (Table 2).

Limited task complexity: The evaluation is restricted to single-object picking/grasping. It remains to be seen if the same 'primitive-toy' training paradigm can scale to more complex dexterous manipulation tasks (e.g., in-hand rotation, tool use).

strengths: Clear and intuitive motivation drawn from cognitive science, exploring how robots can acquire generalizable manipulation skills by learning from simple shape primitives (toy compositions) instead of large-scale in-domain datasets.
Extensive real-world robotic evaluation on two distinct embodiments: a 7-DoF Franka Panda arm with a parallel gripper and a Unitree H1-2 humanoid robot with multi-finger dexterous hands.
Comprehensive scaling and ablation studies analyzing the impact of training toy diversity, number of demonstrations, primitive types, complexity of toy compositions, and policy network scale.
Great detail provided on the 3D printing and manufacturing process of the physical toys, enhancing the reproducibility of the physical experiments.
weaknesses: Ambiguity in the mask generation pipeline for real-world evaluation: Section E states that a Faster R-CNN detector was trained on 200 annotated toy images and its bounding boxes were fed to SAM 2. It is unclear if this toy-trained detector was used directly to segment the vastly different real-world YCB objects, or if manual/alternative prompting was employed. If the pipeline relies on general-purpose zero-shot capabilities of SAM 2 / prompt engineering for YCB, the claim of learning solely from 'random toys' is partially diminished.

Loss of fine-grained spatial information via DetPool: Mean-pooling all the masked object patch tokens into a single feature vector collapses the 2D spatial layout and local geometry of the object. While this helps remove background distractors, it also discards crucial spatial coordinates necessary for precision grasping. The paper lacks a discussion on how the policy overcomes this geometric collapse to achieve precise grasping.

Modest absolute performance in the real world: Achieving 66.67% success on Franka and 50.77% on the H1-2 humanoid indicates that the zero-shot transfer still leaves a significant gap for practical applications. Larger models pretrained on robotic data and then fine-tuned (such as $\pi_0$-FAST at 76.56%) still outperform the proposed method.

Missing comparisons to standard geometric grasp planners: Since the policy is evaluated on single-object grasping, it would be highly informative to compare LEGO against geometry-based grasp planners (e.g., AnyGrasp or Contact-GraspNet) to determine if a learned behavioral cloning policy offers superior robustness or generalization over classical geometric approaches.

strengths: Compelling and intuitive core concept: Drawing inspiration from cognitive science, the paper demonstrates that training on simple, procedurally generated 'Cezanne toys' (compositions of spheres, cuboids, cylinders, and rings) enables zero-shot generalization to complex real-world objects.

Rigorous real-world validation: The authors actually 3D-printed the 250 procedural toys to collect 1,500 real demonstrations on a Franka Panda and 500 on a humanoid Unitree H1-2 with dexterous hands. Testing zero-shot on 64 real YCB objects and 13 everyday objects is a standard-setting level of physical robot evaluation.

Simple and highly effective method: The proposed Detection Pooling (DetPool) mechanism uses SAM 2 to mask attention inside the ViT and mean-pool only target object tokens. This simple architectural detail is shown to be the linchpin for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, boosting success rates by 22-48% over standard pooling methods.

Exceptional thoroughness in ablation and scaling studies: The paper provides extensive scaling curves for demonstration count, object diversity, model sizes, and complexity, alongside robustness analyses against visual distractors, clutter, lighting variations, and mask noise.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on a foreground segmentation mask: The DetPool mechanism assumes access to a reliable object mask (using SAM 2 tracked via a bounding box detector in real-world setups). While the paper demonstrates robustness to mask noise (down to 60% IoU), failure of the primary detector or tracker in highly cluttered or occluded environments will directly impact policy success.

Primarily tailored to grasping: While the appendix introduces a 'push-to-target' task, the core paradigm of learning from simple primitive shapes is naturally optimized for rigid-object grasping. It remains unclear how well this primitive-composition philosophy translates to highly semantic or articulation-heavy tasks (e.g., opening drawers, manipulating deformables, or tool-use).

Finetuned larger baselines still outperform: In the real-robot Franka evaluation (Table 2), a larger VLA model (pi0-FAST, 3B parameters) finetuned on the same toy demonstrations achieves a 76.56% success rate, which is about 10% higher than LEGO (66.67%). While LEGO is vastly more efficient (86M parameters, no large-scale robot pretraining), this shows that pretraining remains highly valuable when combined with toy-based data.

strengths: Compelling and psychologically grounded concept: The core idea of training robot policies exclusively on simple, randomly assembled primitive shapes ("Cezanne toys") to achieve zero-shot generalization on complex real-world objects is elegant and highly practical for data collection.

Rigorous real-robot and humanoid experiments: The authors evaluate their approach on physical platforms, including a 7-DoF Franka Panda robot (on 64 YCB objects) and a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with 12-joint dexterous hands (on 13 everyday objects). The physical evaluation is exceptionally thorough for a robotics paper.

Excellent ablation and scaling studies: The paper provides extensive analyses, including the scaling effects of toy diversity vs. number of demonstrations, the impact of specific primitive shapes, toy complexity, geometric/color diversity, robustness to visual changes (clutter, distractors, lighting), and control parameterization.

Strong performance and data efficiency: The proposed LEGO model (86M parameters) significantly outperforms much larger foundation models (OpenVLA, π0-FAST) in zero-shot settings despite being trained on a fraction of the data.
weaknesses: Moderate technical novelty of DetPool: Restricting attention in Vision Transformers (ViTs) using an object mask and performing mean pooling over the masked patch tokens is a straightforward technique. While highly effective here, the architectural contribution itself is somewhat incremental.

Dependency on accurate object segmentation: The system relies on SAM 2 or a trained object detector to generate masks. Although the authors present a robustness analysis under mask noise, failures in the upstream detection/segmentation model in complex, open-world scenes could limit the overall robustness of the pipeline.

Performance gap compared to fine-tuned foundation models: While LEGO outperforms zero-shot baselines, Table 2 shows that fine-tuned π0-FAST still achieves the highest overall performance (76.56% vs 66.67%). This indicates that large-scale pretraining on diverse robot datasets still holds a notable advantage over learning from scratch on toys.

Focus primarily on single-object grasping: Although the authors demonstrate one push-to-target task in the appendix, the main methodology and evaluation are tailored around pick-and-place. It remains to be seen how well this primitive-shape paradigm generalizes to complex, contact-rich, or multi-object manipulation tasks.

strengths: Intriguing and well-motivated core concept: drawing inspiration from developmental psychology, the paper leverages simple primitive shape compositions ('Cezanne toys') to train grasping policies that successfully generalize to complex, unseen real-world objects.

Extensive physical robot validation: the proposed method is evaluated not only in simulation but also on a 7-DoF Franka Panda robot (64 YCB objects) and, highly impressively, on a Unitree H1-2 humanoid robot with 6-DoF dexterous hands.

Remarkable data and parameter efficiency: with only 86M parameters and trained on a modest dataset of 1,500 real demonstrations, the model achieves highly competitive results against giant, pretrained VLA baselines (3B and 7B parameters) that leverage massive robot pretraining.

Thorough ablation studies: the authors provide a very rich set of evaluations, investigating variables such as the number of toys vs. demonstrations, primitive exclusions, toy complexity, geometric similarity, color diversity, mask noise, and alternative tasks (push-to-target).
weaknesses: Limited novelty in the visual pooling mechanism: the proposed DetPool mechanism (using segmentation masks to mask out cross-attention in ViT and performing mean pooling over object tokens) is a standard design pattern in object-centric computer vision and does not represent a major technical breakthrough.

Critical dependency on external segmenters: the system relies heavily on segmenting the target object (using SAM 2 or Faster R-CNN). Although the authors ablated mask noise down to 60% IoU, errors or complete failures in the segmentation pipeline in cluttered, reflective, or transparent environments will heavily degrade the policy's performance.

Finetuned baselines still outperform in certain setups: on the real Franka robot, the finetuned version of the 3B-parameter π0-FAST model achieves 76.56% success, which is higher than the 66.67% of LEGO. While LEGO does not use any large-scale pretraining, the claims about outperforming state-of-the-art models should be carefully qualified.

High physical overhead for dataset collection: 3D printing 250 unique toys and manually teleoperating 1,500 successful trajectories represents a very labor-intensive pipeline, which could present a bottleneck for other labs attempting to reproduce or scale this setup.
